_comment: The tunes the SH-2 synth carries, and the exact settings each is converted
with. Hand-edited: this is the file to change when a tune plays too fast, is
voiced wrong, or should be cut shorter -- the way castle-halls-drums.tab is
the file to change when a drum strike is in the wrong place.
Read by tools/assets/mid2pat.py --manifest, which emits every tune into one
saturn/src/sound/music_synth_data.c, and by tools/assets/songs.bat, which
renders one of them through the offline model so a change can be heard in a
second without a build.
Fields. id: what songs.bat and the generated C name it by. name and source:
what the generated file credits. midi: relative to this folder. grid: rows
per whole note, 32 unless a tune has nothing finer than a sixteenth to say.
bpm: 0 takes the file's own declared tempo, which is right for every fan
sequence here except castle-halls, whose transcriber wrote it at the wrong
speed. fold: collapse an octave doubling to one voice ('up' keeps the upper
member), which is what a sequencer's thickened bass line costs on three
voices. max_rows: 0 is the whole piece. drums_tab / tab_beats: an authored
drum part that replaces the sequence's own drum channel.
About the max_rows figures. Every tune longer than 48 seconds is cut to 48,
which is twice the length of the shipped default and long for a loop the
player hears while reading one room. It buys 15,060 bytes of the netbin's
image -- sgover.mid alone is 131 seconds and 14,377 bytes uncut, more than a
quarter of the whole catalogue -- and 300 KB is what the loader takes.
They are blind cuts at a number of seconds, NOT at a musical boundary, so a
tune may well end mid-phrase and loop badly. Listen with songs.bat and move
the number: the row grid is 32nds, a bar of 4/4 is 128 rows and a bar of 3/4
is 96, so nudging a cut to the nearest multiple is one edit. castle-halls'
384 is what a deliberate cut looks like -- one statement of the theme.
The titles were read off the filenames of a fan sequence set until each
MIDI was measured against a rip of the NES original -- chroma correlation
over transposition, tempo and offset, by tools/match_nes_rips.py, recorded
in music/nes_refs.json -- and three of them were wrong: sgover.mid is Game
Over and not an overworld, sghalls.mid is Hall of Mirrors, and sglitrod.mid
is Twilight. sglake.mid and shadow7.mid are the SAME PIECE sequenced twice
(0.73 against each other, both matching Subterranean Cavern), so the
catalogue carries one tune in two slots for 6,871 bytes of the netbin image;
dropping one is the owner's call. sgmirror.mid matches nothing in the rip
set at any tempo from 0.4x to 2.6x and is still unidentified. They are
still not Masuno's own titles.
levels: a DISDL level per voice, [bass, lead, harmony, drums], where the
global CH_VOL in mid2pat.py does not suit this arrangement. Three bits and
about 6 dB a step, which is the only per-voice dial the chip has. Measured
the same way: lake's lead reads 0.260 of its energy in the 440-880 Hz
octave where the NES original reads 0.178, and one step down puts it on
0.131 with every other band moving toward the original too. It is per tune
and not global because dropping the lead a step for everyone takes
castle-halls from 0.16 to 0.54 and corridor from 0.15 to 0.53 -- a
sequence that holds its lead longer is a louder lead at the same level,
and that is the sequence's property, not the voicing's.
octaves: a whole-octave correction per tonal lane, [bass, lead, harmony],
for a sequence that wrote a voice in the wrong octave. Measured, not
chosen -- tools/assets/voicecmp.py scores our render's octave-band profile
against the rip's, and the three set here each converge on the original
band by band rather than merely score better. Do not put one on the
percussion lane: that note is the shift register's clock rate.
sgdragon.mid
is damaged -- it declares eight tracks, carries five, and the last of those
ends 290 bytes past the end of the file -- so what converts is the four and a
half tracks that are really there.
default is the tune played where nothing has chosen one: the boot menus, the
netbin, and any room the mood table does not reach.
cd: whether the CD build carries this tune IN ITS IMAGE. Exactly one does,
and every tune is on the disc regardless -- mid2pat.py --pat writes all
twelve into cd/data/BG/MUSIC.PAT and the console reads them one at a time.
The distinction is where the bytes come from. On the CD target
__heap_start follows .rodata, so a tune in the image is taken straight out
of the HWRAM heap the story is loaded into: all twelve there took that heap
to 98,016 and stopped LURKING.Z3 -- 129,704 bytes -- from loading at all. A
tune on the disc costs Low Work RAM instead, which the story does not touch,
and only one tune's worth of it: the catalogue is 41,708 bytes and the Low
Work RAM left in the worst in-game case is 25,998, so what is resident is one
slot the size of the largest tune (8,192) plus a header sector.
The one marked tune is the fallback the build cannot be without: the boot
menus play before the drive has been read, and a disc with no MUSIC.PAT --
or a scratched one -- still has music. Marking a second costs the story heap
its pattern data for no gain the disc file does not already give, so do not,
unless the point is to have a tune that never seeks.
The netbin has no disc and no story, links all twelve, and is bounded by
PlanetWeb's 300 KB instead.
